analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and nursing homes to use mechanical lifts and safety programs instead of manually lifting patients.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 21 House sponsors and no Republican support, was referred to three committees and died without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Labor to write a workplace safety standard requiring health care employers to use mechanical lifting equipment and safety programs when moving patients, rather than having workers lift patients by hand. It would have covered hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and similar facilities, tied compliance to Medicare participation, given workers a right to refuse unsafe lifting assignments, and required unannounced inspections. Nursing assistants and registered nurses report among the highest rates of back and muscle injuries of any occupation, mostly from moving patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Direct-care registered nurses, nursing assistants, and other health care workers who lift, transfer, and reposition patients by hand and suffer high rates of back and muscle injuries. Patients also benefit, because mechanical lifts reduce drops, skin tears, and pressure ulcers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nurses and nursing assistants injured lifting patients

how_it_helps.text: In 2014, registered nurses ranked sixth among all occupations for musculoskeletal injuries causing days away from work, with 11,360 cases, and nursing assistants reported 20,020 cases, the second highest of any profession; the leading cause is lifting, transferring, and repositioning patients.

The bill requires health care employers to develop a safe patient handling program, buy and maintain mechanical lifting equipment, train workers annually, track injury data, and let workers refuse assignments they reasonably believe would violate the standard.

Facilities that adopted safe patient handling technology reported sharp declines in staff injuries, lost work days, and turnover, and studies show it reduces workers' compensation costs for these injuries.
The bill applies the standard to hospitals and other facilities receiving Medicare and Medicaid funds, and directs the Labor Department to conduct unannounced inspections to verify compliance.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other health care employers bear the cost of buying and maintaining lifting equipment, training staff, and running compliance programs within two years of the standard taking effect.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and health care employers

drawbacks.text: Health care employers would face substantial upfront costs to purchase mechanical lift equipment for every patient care area within two years, retrain staff annually, and run data-tracking and annual evaluation programs.

In some patient situations mechanical lifting is not feasible, so the standard permits alternative manual controls when equipment cannot be used, which leaves judgment calls about patient safety to individual facilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to employers are real but front-loaded, and the bill's own findings note that facilities adopting this technology have seen injury, turnover, and workers' compensation costs fall, meaning much of the equipment cost is recovered over time. The main honest objection is the compliance burden on smaller facilities like home health agencies and rural clinics, which the bill does not exempt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2015, referred to three House committees and then to subcommittees, and no committee ever held a hearing or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Conyers Jr. introduced the bill on December 16, 2015, joined by 20 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.

The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means Committees, and it was then referred to the Health and Workforce Protections subcommittees in early 2016.
No further action was taken and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, nursing homes, and other health care employers avoided a federal mandate to buy lifting equipment and run safety programs, and workers who lift patients continued to face the injury rates the bill was written to reduce.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers who avoided the mandate

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Judiciary Committee ranking member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the Democratic cosponsor list.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup in any of the three committees it was sent to.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committees took no action on it.

industries.note: They would have had to buy and maintain mechanical lifting equipment, train staff, and run compliance programs within two years, but the bill's findings note that facilities using this technology have seen injuries, lost work days, turnover, and workers' compensation costs fall, offsetting some of the outlay. Their resistance to a safety mandate runs against the workers and patients the equipment protects.

A mandate that every covered facility purchase and maintain safe patient handling equipment creates a large guaranteed market for lift devices and accessories. The bill's findings state this technology has made manual patient handling largely unnecessary.

industries.industry: Home health agencies and small clinics
industries.note: They are covered as health care employers and would face the same equipment, training, and recordkeeping requirements as large hospital systems, with no small-business exemption in the bill.
